Scanner Benchmark Field Report
Consiva AI · Competitive Field Report

Who else scans Indian websites for DPDP, and how good are they?

We ran four publicly accessible competitor scanners against the same domain Consiva had just scanned, on the same day, and read the official pages of thirteen more. This is what came back.

01

The headline

Four scanners. One website. One day. Four different scores, built on wildly different amounts of evidence — and not one of them tells the reader that the number is not comparable to anyone else's.

What this actually proves

A score out of 100 from a public website scan is not a measurement — it is a house style. The same site is 29, 29, 37.5 and 50 depending on whose checklist you use, how many pages were read, and whether JavaScript was executed. Three of the four read a single page. None discloses that its number is incomparable.

This is the strongest possible argument for the methodology change already proposed for Consiva: show a readiness band with coverage and evidence confidence beside it, and keep the number for Deep Scan, where ownership is verified and coverage is high enough to make it mean something. Competing on the number means competing in a race that has no finish line and no referee.

02

How this was done, and what was not done

Every claim in this report carries a grade. The grades are the point: a benchmark that blurs "we tested it" into "their website says so" is worth nothing in a product decision.

Hands-on

We operated the tool end to end as an ordinary visitor and recorded what came back. Four scanners: checkdpdp.in, seccomply.net, mylegalpal.com, openproof.io.

Documented

Read from the vendor's own official pages, with URL and date. Thirteen further India vendors and seven global CMP vendors.

Claimed

Asserted publicly by the vendor but not independently verifiable — above all, cookie-database sizes.

Not accessible

cotrust.in blocks automated retrieval through robots.txt. Needs a human to open it in a browser before the benchmark is closed.

Three things we deliberately did not do

  • We did not submit dpdpweb.in's form. Its free check requires a work email and sits behind a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge. Entering personal data into a third party's form and engaging a bot-detection challenge are both out of bounds. Its capabilities here are read from its own pages and published sample report.
  • We did not take any paid trial or access any paid tier. Where a vendor publishes only "contact sales", that is recorded as such and not estimated.
  • We did not bypass anything. No CAPTCHA, no WAF, no authentication, no rate limit. Automated access to competitor hosts from the analysis sandbox was refused at the network gateway, so all hands-on work went through an ordinary interactive browser.

Strategic read

Consiva has been fighting two different wars with one product. The enterprise India vendors are Deep Scan and platform competitors — demo-gated, unpriced, no public scanner. The Quick Scan battle is against ten small tools, most of which read a single page, cite sections loosely, and still convert better than Consiva does because they hand over a PDF in ten seconds with no signup.

The result page is addressable by URL, so every scan is shareable by construction. The scan-quality strip is honest about being partial — and then immediately undermined by a confident red 29. Note the four outputs sitting beside the score: Download PDF, Share report, Email me PDF, Re-scan, all before any account exists.

Findings carry an Act section chip, a severity, and an effort estimate — "1 hour", "1–2 days", "half day", "5 minutes". That last column is cheap to build and does real work: it converts a list of problems into a plan a developer can pick up on Monday.

“No banner means trackers run without consent — Section 6 violation.”

checkdpdp.in, finding 1, from a single-page observation

A technical observation on one page, rendered as a statutory violation. Its own disclaimer says the report is "technical guidance, not formal legal counsel", and its meta description offers a "publicly verifiable DPDP certificate". It also leaked an internal failure state to the customer: "Findings generated from deterministic rules only — the LLM key pool was unavailable."

TakeInstant ungated PDF, share and re-scan beside the score. Effort estimates per fix. Domain personalised into the upgrade headline ("Protect bricscci.com in under 10 minutes — free"), placed above the score rather than at the foot of the page. URL-addressable results.
AvoidLegal conclusions from technical signals. Certificate language. A confident score from one page. Internal failure states on a customer surface.

A band legend printed directly under the score — "0–40 High Risk · 41–70 Developing · 71–100 Mature" — plus three honest counters: 1 Pages read · 1 Checks passed · 5 Priority fixes. Telling the reader you read one page, right next to the score, is more candid than most of this field manages.

This is the most important screenshot in the report. Two things to study.

Left: every priority fix carries a paired citation — Section 5(1) - Rule 3, Section 5(1)(i)-(ii) - Rule 3(1), Section 8(10) - Section 13 - Rule 9, Sections 11 to 13 - Rule 13, Section 14. Act and Rule, on every row. This is the only competitor doing what Consiva already does.

Right, and this is the lesson: a dedicated "Not applicable (excluded from scoring)" panel. "No non-essential trackers or cookies detected, so a consent banner is not required for this surface." "No consent banner required on this surface." Each exclusion is named, reasoned and visibly kept out of the score. It then states its own blind spots plainly: it cannot see behind a login, and "banners and tags that render only after JavaScript execution are inferred from markup… not from a rendered page."

A competitor that reads one page without executing JavaScript handles not-applicable findings more rigorously than Consiva's current report does.

Consiva renders "Failed" and "Not tested" in the same row; SecComply gives exclusions their own panel
TakeThe excluded-from-scoring panel, as a first-class report element. Band legend printed beside the score. Pages-read counter next to the number. Plain statement of method limits ("inferred from markup, not a rendered page").
AvoidNothing serious. The weakness is depth, not honesty: one page, no rendering, no consent-state testing.

The gate is the cost of entry here: website address and work email, with a Cloudflare Turnstile beneath. That is a real conversion tax, and it is why Consiva should gate the artefact rather than the insight. But look at what it is protecting.

This is the methodological benchmark for the whole market, and it is the one capability Consiva should be building toward.

  • "Consent at a glance" across four states — 1 · No choice, 2 · Accept all, 3 · Reject all, 4 · Accept, then Reject. The fourth state tests withdrawal, which maps directly to DPDP s.6(4) — consent must be as easy to withdraw as to give.
  • Verdict language instead of raw counts — "Should be 0", "Expected". A reader with no privacy training can tell which column is wrong.
  • A clean Not tested with a stated reason on the withdrawal column: "No Manage cookie choices link or revisit button was found, so the choice could not be reopened." Not a failure. Not a blank. A reason.
  • Header facts: "7 pages · 3 consent states · 25 checks · CookieYes banner detected". The CMP is named.
  • "198 Days to 13 May 2027" rendered as one metric tile among four, not as a fear countdown.
  • Tabs for Fix list 8 · Consent test 3 · Consent Mode v2 1 · Forms 2 · Notices 5.
TakeThe four-state consent panel, verdict language, and a reasoned Not-tested state. This is the single capability that decides whether Consiva's Deep Scan is differentiated or just longer.
AvoidThe email-plus-CAPTCHA gate before any result. Measured against an ungated competitor giving away a PDF in ten seconds, it loses the top of the funnel.

The progress experience is the best in the field and the cheapest thing on this page to copy. A live checklist fills in item by item — HTTPS, SSL certificate, privacy policy, grievance officer, cookie consent tool, third-party trackers, security headers — with running, done and pending states, and an honest line underneath: "Checking security headers… Large sites can take up to a minute." No invented percentage. No creeping bar.

Then the result, and two decisions worth stealing outright.

  • No score at all. "3 of 7 checks passed on bricscci.com", with the caveat "Automatic signals from your public pages. Not a compliance verdict." Where Consiva agonises over 37.5, OpenProof simply refuses the number — and the result reads as more confident, not less.
  • A dependency-blocked state, shipped. Look at Grievance officer named → No policy to read, rendered in grey. That is exactly the BLOCKED_BY_PREREQUISITE pattern Consiva has specified but not built: a check that cannot be evaluated because a prerequisite artefact is missing, shown as neither pass nor fail.
  • Per-check detail values carry information rather than verdicts: 78 days left on the SSL certificate, 3 missing on headers, None detected on trackers.
  • The call to action is a six-step wizard — Scan → About you → Assessment → Consent → Headers → Save — framed as "We found 2 things to fix… First we need to understand your business, so the fixes fit you."
TakeThe live per-check progress feed. "N of M checks passed" instead of a score. The grey prerequisite-blocked state. A staged wizard instead of a bare Sign Up button.
AvoidSeven checks is thin, and no DPDP provision is cited anywhere — the credibility ceiling is low with a privacy professional.

The weakest method and, in one respect, the best writing. Citations are glossed rather than dropped: "DPDP Act 2023, s.5 — notice to the Data Principal", "s.6 — consent must be free, informed and prior". A non-lawyer learns something from every row.

It is also unusually candid about its own blind spot, inside the finding itself: "Note: banners loaded by JavaScript may not be detected by this scan." And the summary is framed correctly — "This is an automated signal scan, not a compliance verdict."

The score tells the real story about this market, though. The same site scored 29 by two tools and 50 here, because this one never executed JavaScript and therefore never looked for most of what the others failed it on. A higher score from a weaker method.

TakeGlossed citations — the section number and a plain-English clause. The per-finding method caveat, placed inside the finding rather than in a footer.
AvoidScoring a site on server HTML alone. It systematically flatters JavaScript-heavy sites, which is most of the Indian mid-market.

The heaviest gate in the field: name, work email, company name and role before a single result. The page knows this is a problem and argues with the visitor about it — "A quick note: … This is a genuine compliance tool, not a marketing exercise — we just need a way to reach you if your scan uncovers something urgent." When a form needs a paragraph defending itself, the form is the problem.

Findings use internal rule IDs (CON-04, WEB-07, NOT-01) rather than statutory provisions, and the site claims "Every result maps to a specific, checkable rule" — its own rule, not the Act's. The one line worth borrowing is the disclaimer: "It is not a compliance certificate and does not by itself make you compliant."

TakeThe blunt non-certificate disclaimer. The "AI in the scan engine: none" line is an interesting trust play in a market where buyers are wary of hallucinated compliance advice.
AvoidA four-field lead form before any value. Proprietary rule IDs in place of statutory citations — it reads as a scorecard the vendor invented, because it is.
05

The Consiva baseline, read the same way

The same scrutiny, applied to our own output on the same domain on the same day. The honest summary: better evidence, weaker packaging.

Ahead of every competitor

  • Act and Rule on every check — matched only by SecComply
  • A "why this page was chosen" column — unique in the market
  • Explicit non-conclusion language on every finding
  • The network-request caveat: a request does not prove personal data was sent
  • Per-finding evidence excerpts tied to the page read
  • The scoring basis published inside the report
  • 5 pages scanned against 1 for three of the four tools

Behind every competitor

  • No PDF, share, email or re-scan — checkDPDP gives all four, ungated
  • No time-to-result disclosed; rivals finish in under ten seconds
  • "Failed" and "Not tested" in the same row — SecComply and dpdpweb both handle exclusions properly
  • Consent states tabled but never tested
  • No commencement date on Rule citations
  • 209 unscanned pages spent as an apology, not as the upgrade offer
  • A generic "Sign Up" at the foot of the densest page
The uncomfortable part

Three defects in our own report are of a kind no competitor commits. Check 9 reports Failed while its own detail says Not tested, and its narrative asserts analytics activity that the report's own metric tile records as zero. Check 10 awards itself 1 of 1 for evidence traceability on a denominator of one, when checks 1 to 9 produced nine findings. And the recommendations advise fixing banner behaviour on a site that has no banner.

Each is individually checkable by any reader in under a minute, and each sits inside the part of the product that carries the "evidence is the moat" claim.

Seven major CMP vendors, official pages read 5 November 2026. Not one mentions India's DPDP Act. Not one states accept/reject consent-state testing.

iubenda“Start for free”€4.99/site/moNot statedNot statedNot statedNo
Piwik PRONot statedContact salesNot statedYes — explicitNot statedNo

They sell blocking. We should sell verification.

Every one of these vendors describes preventing tags from firing. None describes proving what fired, when, and under which choice. Blocking is a CMP feature. Verification is an evidence product — and evidence is the stated moat.

Do not enter the database race.

13,000 to 45,000,000, spanning three and a half orders of magnitude, none independently verifiable, almost certainly not counting the same thing. Compete instead on verified coverage of what Indian sites actually run, with provenance, confidence and a last-verified date per record.

07

What to build, what to refuse

Adopt — observed working in the field

  1. Four-state consent testing, with a reasoned Not-tested state (dpdpweb)
  2. Live per-check progress feed with an honest slow-site line (OpenProof)
  3. An excluded-from-scoring panel, named and reasoned (SecComply)
  4. A grey prerequisite-blocked state — neither pass nor fail (OpenProof)
  5. Ungated PDF, share, email and re-scan beside the result (checkDPDP)
  6. Effort estimates per fix (checkDPDP)
  7. Glossed citations — section number plus plain-English clause (My Legal Pal)
  8. Pages-read counter beside the score, and a printed band legend (SecComply)
  9. Domain personalised into the upgrade headline, placed above the fold (checkDPDP)
  10. A staged wizard rather than a bare Sign Up (OpenProof)

Refuse — regardless of what it does for conversion

  1. Legal conclusions from technical signals — “Section 6 violation”
  2. Certificate, badge or seal language of any kind
  3. A confident score from a single page with no disclosure
  4. Fear hooks — gavels, red alerts, “₹250 crore per breach”
  5. Scoring a site on server HTML without executing JavaScript
  6. Proprietary rule IDs standing in for statutory citations
  7. Multi-field lead forms before any value is delivered
  8. Internal failure states on a customer surface
  9. Cookie-database size as a marketing number
  10. Any implication of Consent Manager registration under Rule 4
On Consent Manager claims

No vendor in this field claims registration. Leegality's "India's first DPDP Act compliant Consent Manager" headline sits closest to the line; Consentin's own FAQ states there are no registered Consent Managers in India yet. Privista says plainly that it is not one — "No, and deliberately so." That reads as confidence rather than weakness, and it forecloses an attack. Consiva should consider saying the same, in the same words.

The conclusion in one line

Consiva is technically superior and legally sounder on every dimension that matters, and commercially weaker on every dimension the visitor experiences first. Nothing in the Behind column is hard to build. Everything in the Ahead column took real judgement and would take a competitor a long time to copy. That is a good position to be in — provided the packaging gap is closed before the market commoditises.

09

Open items

What this fieldwork could not settle, so that nobody treats the benchmark as finished.

  • cotrust.in — robots.txt disallows automated retrieval. Needs a human in a browser.
  • dpdpweb's live output — read from its published sample only. Its four-state panel should be confirmed against a real run, from a company mailbox, by a person.
  • Paid tiers — none accessed anywhere. The paid columns in the global table are vendor documentation, not observation.
  • Six further India tools — consentx.io, thedataprivacy.cloud, contractshield.in, privista.in, digitalanumati.com and borderastra's actual result page were documented but not operated end to end.
  • Consiva's published pricing — not supplied with this work, so the commercial comparison is anchored on competitor prices alone.
  • Scores move. Every number here is a 5 November 2026 observation of a live tool. Re-run before quoting in a deck.
